result.party_text: The claimant said he signed forms the next day without interpretation because he was asked to, and was in a poor mental state during immigration interviews.
result.answer_quote: However, the Panel cannot accept these explanations. The claimant is a university graduate, and thus should have been able to appreciate the advisability of not signing something, in Canada, just because someone asks him to. Also, the Panel finds that Immigration Canada would not request a refugee claimant to sign something that they knew or should have known not to be true, i.e. that the contents of the form were interpreted to the claimant, although he said at the hearing that they were not. There is a presumption that Canadian Immigration officials deal fairly, openly and honestly with refugee claimants, and insufficient evidence has been provided to rebut this assumption. Thus, in summary, the Panel does not, overall, accept the claimant's explanations of inconsistencies in his evidence to be the result of inadequate interpretation services supplied by Citizenship and Immigration Canada to the claimant.
result.why: The court rejects the claimant's explanation about signing without interpretation and poor mental state, finding the explanations unconvincing.

result.party_text: There are significant inconsistencies in the claimant's evidence regarding the dates of his first detention.
result.answer_quote: The claimant was asked the dates of his first detention. He said they were XXXXX, 2005, to XXXXX 2005. When asked if he was sure, he said yes, except the dates may be off by one day only. It was pointed out to him that he gave the following different dates for his first detention, as follows. In his PIF, section 9, he wrote that it was from XXXXX, 2005 to XXXXX, 2005. In IMM 5474, the Immigration form discussed above, he said it was in a different year entirely, from XXXXX, 2006 to XXXXX, 2006. With respect to IMM 5474, the claimant indicated that this was the second detention, and this will be dealt with below. However, the inconsistency remains between what he said at the hearing and what he had written in the PIF. It was pointed out to the claimant that at the beginning of the hearing, he had sworn to the accuracy of the PIF, and at the hearing he was alleging that it was not correct in this respect. This the claimant blamed on the interpreter at counsel's office. He said this interpreter copied some dates from the interview record with Immigration, and gave examples that the claimant's birthdate was recorded wrong. However, nothing in Exhibit R/A-2 was pointed out wherein the claimant indicated that he had been detained from XXXXX, 2005 to XXXXX, 2005, therefore the Panel cannot accept this explanation that counsel's interpreter incorrectly copied the dates wrong from what is now Exhibit R/A-2. Then counsel got up and showed the Panel a copy she had of the PIF, which appeared to indicate some changes in pen or pencil to section 9 of the PIF. Counsel indicated that this was evidence that she intended to change section 9 of the PIF before the claimant swore to it at the hearing, but forgot due to her illness. The Panel did not clearly see what counsel had notated by hand in her copy of the PIF, nor was it requested to be entered as an Exhibit, and it was not. She indicated correctly that the revised Narrative indicated that the claimant was arrested on XXXXX, 2005. The Panel can to a certain extent understand counsel's point. However, the fact that the claimant, apparently incorrectly, blamed this on the interpreter, and also, apparently incorrectly, indicated that the interpreter had taken the wrong information from Exhibit R/A-2, would tend to indicate that the claimant's explanation should not be accepted. When considering all the above, from this inconsistency, only partially explained satisfactorily, the Panel will make a negative inference as to credibility, although the impact of this finding is partially mitigated by counsel's explanation.
result.why: The court accepts there are significant inconsistencies in the claimant's evidence regarding the dates of his first detention and makes a negative credibility inference.
